title: The boycott
hook: Quraysh boycott the Prophet's clan, who live three years in a valley near starvation

segments.voice: Yesterday, al-Najashi weeps, and the emigrants are safe across the sea. Your line was: the king wept. Who was the guest you looked out for? Day seven hundred forty-five.

No sword, this time. No rock on anyone's chest. Just a sheet of writing. Back in Mecca, Ibn Ishaq says, the leaders of Quraysh saw the Muslims safe in Abyssinia, saw Hamzah and Umar on the Prophet's side, and saw the message spreading among the clans. So they tried something slower. They drew up a document, agreed to it together, and hung it inside the Ka'ba, to make it binding. It was aimed at one family. Today: the boycott.
screen: `NO SWORD, JUST A DOCUMENT.` → `HUNG INSIDE THE KA'BA.` → `AIMED AT ONE FAMILY.`

segments.voice: The terms, as Ibn Ishaq gives them, were simple. No one would marry into the clans of Hashim and al-Muttalib, or give them anyone in marriage. No one would sell to them, or buy from them. Cut off the family, and the man at its center would be handed over or starve with them. The clan didn't hand him over. Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib went with Abu Talib into his valley on the edge of Mecca, the shi'b, and Ibn Ishaq says they went together, believers and unbelievers alike. Abu Lahab, Ibn Ishaq says, left his clan and sided with Quraysh. So the boycott shut in people who did not share the Prophet's faith, only his blood. And they went hungry. Ibn Ishaq says they were worn down, and that almost nothing reached them except what was smuggled in. He tells of Hakim ibn Hizam with a servant carrying wheat for his aunt Khadijah, until Abu Jahl caught him and tried to stop it, and another Meccan stepped in and let the food pass. How long did it last? Ibn Ishaq says two or three years; today's line rounds it to three years hungry. A document hung inside the Ka'ba, used to starve a family. The family's answer was to stay together.
screen: `NO MARRIAGE, NO TRADE.` · `INTO THE VALLEY, ALL TOGETHER.` · `BLOOD, NOT ONLY FAITH.` · `WHEAT FOR KHADIJAH.`

segments.voice: The practice: go without one thing, and give it. Sit, and breathe, and think about today. What's one thing you'll eat, drink or buy that you could do without: a coffee, a snack, a delivery, a second helping. Choose it now. Then choose where it goes instead: the money to a food bank, the food to a neighbor, the time to someone who's struggling. Notice the small pull of wanting it anyway. In the valley, that pull lasted for years. If you pray, you can remember the hungry by name. The bell holds the time.
The boycott. Quraysh agree in writing to cut off the Prophet's clan, no marriage and no trade, and the clan holds together in the valley, hungry. Today's word.
Your line: three years hungry. Today, the one thing you went without, give it away before the day is out, and let the small hunger remind you who's hungry for real. Day seven hundred forty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims retell the boycott in sirah lessons as the time the Prophet's clan was confined to the valley of Abu Talib, and point to the clan's loyalty, believers and unbelievers together.

pairs: Abu Talib's valley, where the clan went
the uncle who sided with Quraysh

myth: only the Muslims of the clan were shut in
Ibn Ishaq says believers and unbelievers of Hashim and al-Muttalib went together.
the boycott banned marriage and trade with the clan
no one would marry into them, sell to them or buy from them.
Ibn Ishaq gives an exact length for the boycott
he says two or three years.

fork.setup: you're Abu Talib, head of the clan. the city will starve your clan unless he's handed over. what do you do?
options: hand him over to save the clan.
take the whole clan into the valley with him.
fork.reveal: Ibn Ishaq says Hashim and al-Muttalib went into Abu Talib's valley together, believers and unbelievers alike.

original.note: Arabic: a mountain pass or narrow valley; the shi'b of Abu Talib, where the clan was confined.

trapdoor: what you thought: people stopped shopping somewhere to make a point.
what it means: a written ban on marriage and trade that shut a whole clan, believers and not, into a valley to go hungry.
what a scholar hears: Ibn Ishaq's terms of the document hung in the Ka'ba; Abu Lahab's defection; 'two or three years'.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the document against Banu Hashim and Banu al-Muttalib; the shi'b of Abu Talib; Abu Lahab; Hakim ibn Hizam's wheat; two or three years)

notes: The index carry says 'three years hungry'; Ibn Ishaq says 'two or three years'. The script gives both and frames the carry as how Muslims remember it. Confirm.
'Believers and unbelievers alike' paraphrases Ibn Ishaq; confirm.
The Meccan who let Hakim's wheat pass is Abu al-Bakhtari in Ibn Ishaq; left unnamed here because he belongs to the story of the boycott's end (day 747). Confirm.
The practice suggests giving to a food bank; this is a general charity invitation, not described as sadaqah. Confirm.

Editor: cut 'here's the surprise'; removed the flat statement that Abu Talib 'never became Muslim' (Sunni and Shia traditions read his faith differently, see day 735) here and in the fork; changed 'the one uncle who sided with Quraysh' to Ibn Ishaq's plain report about Abu Lahab; Hakim's wheat now carried by a servant, as in Ibn Ishaq, not a camel; 'Muslims remember it as three years' changed to 'today's line rounds it to three'.
Auditor: read against Ibn Ishaq's account of the document, the shi'b, Abu Lahab and Hakim's wheat; no changes needed.
